newsitem.title: PANAMA: Panama bolsa has bullish H1, more gains seen.
newsitem.headline: Panama bolsa has bullish H1, more gains seen.

text.p: Share prices on Panama's Stock Exchange saw a bullish first half, rising 33.2 percent in much improved volume on the back of domestic investor enthusiasm and confidence in the market as the economy starts to pick up, traders said Thursday.

They added that recent institutional reforms, such as its privatization drive, a Brady-style debt restructuring and Eurobond issue would make foreign investors more attracted to Panama's market, but their entry was still limited by its small size.
"There's a lot of money flow in Panama, and a lot of cash but not enough issues out there to buy," trader Fred Roa at Private Discount Brokers told Reuters.
The market's 11-share general index closed at 370.11 June 30, up from 277.87 at the end of last year. The index gained 25 percent in 1996 as a whole.

The exchange saw a 127 percent jump in volume during the first half of 1997 to $312.7 million, the Stock Exchange Director Roberto Brenes told reporters. He added that almost 50 percent of volume traded were in corporate bond issues.
Trading volume rose 91.3 percent in 1996 to $446.5 million.

Traders said financial stocks had led the bolsa higher in the first half of this year, with Banco del Istmo, Empresa General de Inversiones S.A. and Pribanco among the main gainers. But they said the market's bullish behavior was also felt in most of the 21-traded companies.

"There is such a large demand for limited stocks here, but one way we are helping foreigners access the market is through setting up investment funds," said fund manager Carlos Mendoza at brokerage Wall Street Securities.

He was optimistic about the next six months as structural economic reforms started two years ago start to bear fruit. Panama's Gross Domestic Product in real terms grew 3.6 percent in the first quarter against the same period last year.
A banking law due to be completed in the coming months and the government's efforts to step up regulations in the financial sector to bring more transparency have also been welcomed by investors.

"Privatization is making the labor market more flexible. There has been investment in infrastructure and the share price of Panamanian stocks compared to the rest of Latin America are lower," Mendoza added.

Traders said the problem of limited issues in the market was changing as more private Panamanian firms saw the advantage of listing their companies on the bolsa. "Now that prices have reached more interesting levels the shareholders of private companies are becoming more interested in going public," Mendoza said.

Companies registered with the Panama bolsa totaled 114 on June 30, of which 21 had their shares quoted on the stock market, with a capitalization of $1.735 billion, according to Stock Exchange statistics.
